individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes the Neural Rodrigues Operator, a learnable generalization of the Rodrigues' rotation formula, and builds the Rodrigues Network (RodriNet) that injects kinematic inductive bias into neural networks for action learning. The architecture comprises Rodrigues Layers for joint-to-link propagation, Joint Layers for link-to-joint propagation, self-attention for global exchange, and optional global tokens. The method is evaluated on forward kinematics fitting, Cartesian motion prediction, imitation learning with Diffusion Policy, and 3D hand reconstruction, showing improvements over standard backbones.
Strengths: Novel idea of deriving a learnable operator from forward kinematics to inject kinematic structure as an inductive bias.
Well-designed multi-channel extension and network components (Rodrigues Layer, Joint Layer, self-attention, global token) that balance structural bias with flexibility.
Comprehensive experiments across synthetic and realistic tasks (kinematics, motion prediction, robot manipulation, hand reconstruction) demonstrate consistent performance gains.
Ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis provide insight into the contributions of each architectural component.
Weaknesses: The main formulation assumes 1-DoF revolute joints; the extension to 3-DoF joints (e.g., MANO hand) is relegated to the appendix, which is a significant omission given the hand reconstruction results.
The multi-channel operator mixes joint feature channels via sums of cos/sin terms, which may dilute the physical kinematic interpretation and weaken the claimed degeneracy to forward kinematics.
The architecture is robot-specific (per-joint kernels, fixed kinematic tree), raising concerns about generalization to new embodiments or varying structures without retraining.
Imitation learning improvements are modest and task-dependent; the paper does not deeply analyze why the backbone is the bottleneck in some tasks but not others.
The hand reconstruction gains over HaMeR are small (e.g., PA-MPVPE 5.6 vs 5.7) and may lack statistical significance; also, the comparison includes only a subset of recent methods.
Questions: How does the Rodrigues Operator handle multi-DoF joints in the main architecture, and is the quaternion extension in the appendix considered a core contribution?
Can RodriNet be applied to a new robot with a different kinematic structure without retraining per-joint kernels?
In Equation (6), the joint feature vector is transformed elementwise via cos/sin and summed over channels; what is the physical interpretation of this operation?
What is the role of the global token in imitation learning, and how does it interact with the kinematic tree?
How sensitive is the method to inaccuracies in the kinematic model (joint axes, link offsets), and are the learnable weights initialized to the true forward-kinematics parameters?
Limitations: The method requires a known kinematic structure and per-joint kernels, limiting generalization to unseen robot morphologies.
The primary formulation only handles revolute joints; translational joints are not addressed.
Link geometry (lengths, shapes) is ignored, which may be important for contact-rich tasks.
The custom CUDA kernel is not released, and its complexity may hinder adoption.
The improvement in hand reconstruction is marginal, and the comparison may not include all recent state-of-the-art methods.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes the Neural Rodrigues Operator, a learnable generalization of Rodrigues' rotation formula, and builds the Rodrigues Network (RodriNet) that injects kinematic inductive bias into neural networks for action learning. RodriNet consists of Rodrigues Layers, Joint Layers, and Self-Attention Layers, and is evaluated on forward kinematics fitting, Cartesian motion prediction, imitation learning with Diffusion Policy, and 3D hand reconstruction. Results show improvements over standard backbones, with the largest gains in the synthetic tasks and modest improvements in realistic applications.
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated operator derived from forward kinematics, providing a new way to inject kinematic inductive bias into neural networks.
Comprehensive evaluation across four diverse tasks, including synthetic and realistic scenarios, with consistent improvement over standard backbones (MLP, GCN, Transformer, BoT).
Ablation studies confirm the importance of the Rodrigues Layer, supporting the claim that the kinematic prior is responsible for the gains.
Demonstrates generality by applying the architecture to 3D hand reconstruction, outperforming a strong baseline (HaMeR) with fewer parameters.
Detailed appendix with hyperparameters, training details, and additional sensitivity analysis.
Weaknesses: The connection to actual forward kinematics is only theoretical; the learned weights are not constrained to match FK, so the inductive bias may be weakened in practice.

Improvements in imitation learning are modest and inconsistent (e.g., PlugCharger shows lower success than UNet-DP), and no comparison to other structure-aware backbones like GCN-based policies is provided.
The hand reconstruction results show a small improvement (0.3 mm) on a single dataset, and the adaptation from 1-DoF joints to MANO's 3-DoF joints is not clearly explained in the main text.
The architecture requires per-joint parameters, limiting generalization to different robots or embodiments without retraining.

The paper is dense and sometimes hard to follow, especially the multi-channel operator definition and the integration with image features in hand reconstruction; some key details are only in the appendix.
Questions: In the hand reconstruction experiments, is the quaternion-based operator from Appendix A used? How are the 3-DoF joints of MANO handled?
What observation space is used in the imitation learning experiments? If only state-based observations are used, how does the UNet-DP baseline (designed for image inputs) perform?
Is there any initialization of the learned weights to approximate the true forward kinematics, or does the network start from random initialization?
What is the inference-time computational cost of RodriNet compared to the baselines, especially with the CUDA kernel?
Limitations: Assumes a fixed known kinematic tree; cannot handle unknown or changing structures.
Designed for revolute 1-DoF joints; other joint types require further extension.
Experiments are limited to simulation and one hand dataset; no real-world robotic evaluation.
Self-attention layers may not be necessary for all tasks and can slightly reduce test performance (as shown in ablation).
The per-joint parameterization may lead to a large number of parameters for high-DoF systems, though the paper shows parameter efficiency in some cases.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes a Neural Rodrigues Operator, a learnable generalization of the Rodrigues' rotation formula, to inject kinematics-aware inductive bias into neural networks for articulated action learning. Building on this operator, the authors design the Rodrigues Network (RodriNet), which includes Rodrigues Layers, Joint Layers, and Self-Attention Layers. The method is evaluated on synthetic forward kinematics fitting, Cartesian motion prediction, imitation learning with Diffusion Policy on robotic manipulation tasks, and 3D hand reconstruction, showing improvements over several baselines.
Strengths: The idea of deriving a learnable operator from Rodrigues' formula is novel and provides a principled way to inject kinematic inductive bias.
The synthetic experiments show large improvements over MLP/GCN/Transformer/BoT, even with much fewer parameters in FK fitting, demonstrating expressivity.
The paper includes extensive ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, increasing confidence in the architecture's design.
The approach is applied to both robot learning and hand reconstruction, showing versatility.
The custom CUDA implementation for the multi-channel operator addresses practical efficiency concerns.
Weaknesses: The link from the derived operator to actual performance is not fully explained; the learned weights are far from the original FK coefficients, so it is unclear what kinematic structure is preserved after learning.
In imitation learning, the gains are modest and inconsistent across tasks (e.g., PlugCharger is worse than UNet-DP), and no statistical significance testing is reported.
The hand reconstruction experiment changes multiple components (backbone, cross-attention) relative to HaMeR, so the improvement cannot be attributed solely to the Rodrigues operator.
The quaternion extension in Appendix A is not evaluated separately, and it introduces many extra weights, making the approach less elegant.
The comparison against other structure-aware methods (e.g., Body Transformer) is only in toy tasks, not in realistic benchmarks.
The paper does not provide a controlled ablation on FreiHAND that isolates the effect of the Rodrigues operator from other architectural changes.
Questions: Can you provide statistical significance tests (e.g., confidence intervals or p-values) for the imitation learning success rates, especially for PickCube and StackCube?

What is the contribution of the Rodrigues operator in hand reconstruction? Please ablate by replacing only the transformer backbone with RodriNet while keeping cross-attention fixed, and an additional ablation without cross-attention.
How does the network handle joints with limited ranges? Does the inductive bias depend on the specific robot structure at initialization?
What is the memory and computational cost for a high-DoF humanoid (e.g., 30+ joints) compared to a Transformer of similar capacity?
Why is the global token needed for gripper action prediction? What information does it encode?
In the toy motion prediction task, joint ranges are limited to ensure unique IK. How does this restriction affect the generalizability of the conclusions to full-range motion?
Limitations: The method only considers 1-DoF revolute joints; extending to 3-DoF joints requires a separate quaternion-based operator with many parameters.
Link geometry is ignored; only joint connectivity is used, which may limit contact-rich tasks.
Robot experiments are limited to simulation and relatively small demonstration sets.
The custom CUDA kernel is not yet optimized to the level of standard operators, which may hinder adoption.
No real-world robotic experiments are conducted.
The hand reconstruction experiment uses multiple training datasets, and the comparison to prior methods may not be fully controlled for training data or computational budget.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces the Neural Rodrigues Operator, a learnable generalization of Rodrigues' rotation formula designed to inject kinematic inductive bias into neural networks for articulated action learning. The authors build the Rodrigues Network (RodriNet) using this operator, along with a Joint Layer and Self-Attention Layer, and evaluate it on forward kinematics fitting, Cartesian motion prediction, imitation learning with Diffusion Policy, and 3D hand reconstruction. The results show that RodriNet substantially outperforms standard backbones on synthetic kinematic tasks, achieves state-of-the-art performance on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks, and improves hand reconstruction accuracy on FreiHand while using significantly fewer parameters.
Strengths: The Neural Rodrigues Operator is a novel and principled way to encode kinematic structure, derived directly from the forward kinematics formulation, and the multi-channel extension makes it applicable to modern neural architectures.

Strong empirical results on toy tasks: RodriNet fits forward kinematics and predicts Cartesian motion with much lower error than MLP/GCN/Transformer baselines, even with an order of magnitude fewer parameters.
The method is demonstrated on two realistic applications (imitation learning and hand reconstruction), showing broad applicability to articulated systems beyond robots.

The paper includes thorough ablations (removing Rodrigues/Joint/Self-Attention layers) and parameter-scaling experiments for baselines, supporting the claim that the kinematic inductive bias is the key contributor.
The hand reconstruction results achieve state-of-the-art on FreiHand with a 3.7x reduction in parameters compared to HaMeR, suggesting parameter efficiency.
Weaknesses: The imitation learning gains are modest (average success 0.61 vs 0.58 for UNet-DP) and the method underperforms UNet-DP on PlugCharger (0.10 vs 0.13). No statistical significance tests are reported, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not robustly supported.
In hand reconstruction, the improvement over HaMeR is small (e.g., 0.2-0.3 mm in PA-MPJPE/PA-MPVPE) and no variance or multiple-seed results are provided; the difference may be within noise.

The adaptation of the Rodrigues operator to MANO's 3-DoF joints (through quaternion-based extension) is only described in the Appendix, making it hard to judge the main paper's claim of applicability to hand reconstruction without reading the supplementary material.
The custom CUDA kernel is crucial for training efficiency, but source code is not provided, which could limit reproducibility and practical adoption.

The paper does not discuss how the kinematic tree structure is specified or whether the method can handle variations in robot morphology across tasks; each joint has its own learned kernels, which may require retraining for new embodiments.
Questions: How are the Rodrigues Kernels initialized, and does the initialization scheme significantly affect convergence and final performance?
In the imitation learning experiments, what are the confidence intervals or p-values for the differences in success rates across seeds? Are the observed improvements statistically significant?

For the hand reconstruction experiments, what specific modifications are made to the Rodrigues Layer to handle 3-DoF joint rotations? Does the quaternion-based operator in Appendix A yield the same performance as a simpler approach?

How is the kinematic tree structure encoded in the network (e.g., as a fixed graph given at initialization), and can the network be applied to a different robot without retraining the joint-specific parameters?
What is the inference-time computational cost of RodriNet compared to the baselines, especially in the imitation learning setting?
Limitations: The method focuses on joint-level kinematics but ignores link geometry (lengths and shapes), which may limit performance on tasks requiring precise contact reasoning.
The Neural Rodrigues Operator is designed for revolute joints; extending it to translational or helical joints is not addressed.
The evaluation is limited to simulation and single-image reconstruction; real-world robot learning may introduce additional challenges such as sensor noise and system delays.
The classification of the method as 'state-of-the-art' in imitation learning is weakened by the small average improvement and the underperformance on one task.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_5

review.Summary: The paper introduces the Neural Rodrigues Operator, a learnable generalization of the Rodrigues rotation formula, and builds a neural architecture called RodriNet around it. The operator injects a kinematic inductive bias into network layers by replacing the fixed coefficients in forward kinematics with learnable weights, and is extended to multi-channel features. RodriNet consists of Rodrigues Layers, Joint Layers, and Self-Attention Layers, optionally with a global token. The paper evaluates RodriNet on forward kinematics fitting and Cartesian motion prediction (synthetic tasks), imitation learning for robotic manipulation using Diffusion Policy (ManiSkill benchmarks), and single-image 3D hand reconstruction (FreiHAND). The results show large gains over MLP/GCN/Transformer baselines on synthetic tasks and competitive or superior performance on realistic benchmarks.
Strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: deriving a neural operator from the classical Rodrigues formula and injecting kinematic structure as an inductive bias, analogous to how CNNs generalize classical convolution.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains (kinematics, robot learning, hand reconstruction) demonstrates broad applicability and often substantial improvements over generic backbones.
The multi-channel extension and the quaternion-based variant for articulated animated characters (MANO/SMPL) show thoughtful generalization beyond simple 1-DoF revolute joints.
The paper includes detailed ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses in the appendix, supporting the importance of the Rodrigues Layer and robustness of the architecture.
A custom CUDA kernel is developed to make the operator practical, addressing a potential efficiency bottleneck.
Many baselines are compared with controlled parameter counts, and the proposed model often achieves better results with fewer parameters, as in the hand reconstruction case (10.7M vs 39.5M).
Weaknesses: The claimed superiority on realistic tasks is task-dependent: gains are large on PickCube and StackCube but negligible or negative on PlugCharger, and the paper attributes this to contact dynamics without a deeper analysis.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: the Neural Rodrigues Operator is essentially a learnable linear combination of sin/cos features, which may be seen as a special case of Fourier features; a comparison to such a baseline is missing.

The paper does not compare against other structure-aware architectures such as graph convolutional networks with kinematic edges, or Body Transformer (BoT) variants in the large-scale experiments; the GCN/BoT baselines are used only in toy tasks.

The hand reconstruction experiment reports a single run without standard deviations or multiple seeds, making statistical significance unclear; gains over HaMeR are marginal (e.g., PA-MPVPE 5.6 vs 5.9).
There are several typos and writing issues (e.g., 'scaler', 'similarily', 'imaging learning', 'camera') that detract from clarity.
The paper claims 'significant improvements' but the real-world (simulation) gains are moderate, and the architecture is not evaluated in real-world robotic settings.
The theoretical justification for why the rodriNet should generalize better is empirical only; no formal characterization of expressivity or generalization is provided.
Questions: How does the Neural Rodrigues Operator compare to simply using sinusoidal or random Fourier features in an MLP or Transformer? An ablation replacing the Rodrigues kernel with generic trigonometric features would isolate the contribution of the kinematic structure.
Does the RodriNet generalize to previously unseen robot morphologies or kinematic trees? The operator assumes a fixed structure per joint; can the learned kernels be transferred to other embodiments?
What is the effect of the global token on performance? The paper mentions it is optionally enabled, but no ablation is shown for tasks that use it.
How does the method perform under reinforcement learning (RL) rather than imitation learning? The paper lists this as future work, but it is a key limitation for practical robot learning.
Are the reported hand reconstruction results statistically significant? Please provide variance/confidence intervals across multiple seeds.
How sensitive is the model to the ordering of joints/links in the kinematic tree? Would different root choices change performance materially?
The paper uses 18 blocks for hand reconstruction but 12 for other tasks; what is the rationale and sensitivity to depth for the hand task?
Limitations: The method only handles revolute (rotational) joints; extension to prismatic/translational joints is not covered.
Link geometry (lengths, shapes, inertias) is not modeled; the architecture relies only on kinematic tree topology and joint angles.
Robotic experiments are conducted entirely in simulation; real-world deployment remains untested.
Hand reconstruction is evaluated only on FreiHAND; cross-dataset generalization is not assessed.
The custom CUDA kernel is non-standard and may limit reproducibility on other platforms without equivalent optimization.
The paper does not release code or pretrained models, making it harder for the community to reproduce and build upon.

review.Summary: The paper introduces the Neural Rodrigues Operator, a learnable generalization of the Rodrigues' rotation formula, and builds the Rodrigues Network (RodriNet) to inject kinematic inductive bias into neural networks for articulated action learning. The architecture comprises Rodrigues Layers, Joint Layers, and Self-Attention Layers, with optional global tokens. It is evaluated on synthetic forward kinematics fitting, Cartesian motion prediction, imitation learning for robotic manipulation (ManiSkill), and single-image 3D hand reconstruction (FreiHAND). Across five reviews, the method is regarded as novel and well-motivated, showing large gains on synthetic tasks over MLP/GCN/Transformer baselines, and competitive or improved performance on realistic benchmarks, with the strongest advantages in parameter efficiency and kinematic structure utilization. However, reviewers noted that gains on realistic tasks are modest or inconsistent, hand reconstruction improvements are marginal and without statistical significance, the multi-DoF extension is only in the appendix, and the method assumes a fixed known kinematic structure.
Strengths: The Neural Rodrigues Operator is a novel and principled way to inject kinematic inductive bias, derived directly from forward kinematics and generalizable to multi-channel features.

Comprehensive evaluation across four diverse tasks demonstrates broad applicability, with substantial improvements over standard backbones on synthetic kinematic tasks and parameter efficiency in hand reconstruction.
Ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses confirm the importance of the Rodrigues Layer and provide insight into architectural choices.
The multi-channel extension and quaternion-based variant show thoughtful generalization beyond simple 1-DoF revolute joints, enabling use in hand reconstruction.
A custom CUDA kernel addresses practical efficiency, and the paper compares against numerous baselines with controlled parameter counts.
Weaknesses: Improvements on realistic tasks are task-dependent and often modest: imitation learning gains are small (average success 0.61 vs 0.58 for UNet-DP) and RodriNet underperforms UNet-DP on PlugCharger; no statistical significance tests are provided.
Hand reconstruction improvements over HaMeR are marginal (e.g., PA-MPVPE 5.6 vs 5.9) and reported from a single run without variance or multiple seeds, casting doubt on significance.
The adaptation of the operator to 3-DoF MANO joints is relegated to the appendix, and the main text does not clearly explain how the core 1-DoF formulation extends to multi-DoF joints.
The architecture requires a fixed, known kinematic tree with per-joint parameters, limiting generalization to new embodiments or varying structures without retraining.
No comparison to other structure-aware backbones (e.g., GCN with kinematic edges or Body Transformer) in the large-scale experiments; Fourier feature baselines are also missing.
The connection between the learned weights and true forward kinematics is not explored; the inductive bias is not enforced, so the physical interpretation is weakened.
The paper has several writing issues and typos that detract from clarity, and no code or pretrained models are released.
Questions: How does the Neural Rodrigues Operator compare to simply using sinusoidal or random Fourier features in an MLP or Transformer? An ablation replacing the Rodrigues kernel with generic trigonometric features would isolate the contribution of kinematic structure.
Can RodriNet be applied to a new robot with a different kinematic structure without retraining per-joint kernels? Are the learned kernels transferable?
How are the Rodrigues Kernels initialized, and does the initialization scheme significantly affect convergence and final performance?
In the hand reconstruction experiments, is the quaternion-based operator from Appendix A used? How are the 3-DoF joints of MANO handled, and does it yield the same performance as a simpler approach?
What are the statistical significance tests (confidence intervals or p-values) for the imitation learning success rates, especially for PickCube and StackCube?
What is the effect of the global token on performance? The paper mentions it is optionally enabled, but no ablation is shown for tasks that use it.
How does the method perform under reinforcement learning rather than imitation learning? This is listed as future work but is a key limitation for practical robot learning.
How sensitive is the model to inaccuracies in the kinematic model (joint axes, link offsets)?
What is the memory and computational cost for high-DoF humanoids (e.g., 30+ joints) compared to a Transformer of similar capacity?
Limitations: The method assumes a fixed, known kinematic tree and per-joint parameters, limiting generalization to unseen robot morphologies.
The primary formulation only handles 1-DoF revolute joints; translational or helical joints are not addressed, and the multi-DoF extension is not in the main text.
Link geometry (lengths, shapes, inertias) is ignored, which may be important for contact-rich tasks.
Robotic experiments are conducted entirely in simulation; real-world deployment is untested.
Hand reconstruction is evaluated only on FreiHAND, with no cross-dataset generalization assessment.
The custom CUDA kernel is not released and may limit reproducibility or adoption on other platforms.
The paper does not provide formal theoretical justification for why the architecture generalizes better; only empirical evidence is given.
The method currently requires a known kinematic structure, with no mechanism for online adaptation to unknown or changing structures.
